overview:
In the spring of 1967 a Soviet warning to Cairo — false, as it turned out — that Israel was massing troops for an invasion of Syria set off a chain of escalations no one seemed able to stop. Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser poured forces into the Sinai, demanded the withdrawal of the UN peacekeeping force that had stood between Egypt and Israel since 1956, and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, a step Israel had long said it would treat as an act of war. Jordan's King Hussein, who distrusted Nasser, nonetheless signed a mutual defense pact with him on 30 May. Washington tried to organize an international convoy to reopen the straits and failed. On the morning of 5 June, Israel struck first: roughly 200 aircraft flew low over the sea beneath Egyptian radar and destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground, some 300-odd planes in a few hours, before turning on Syrian and Jordanian airfields. Everything that followed took place under Israeli air supremacy.

The ground war was short and brutally lopsided. Israeli armor broke into Sinai through the fortified box at Abu-Ageila and the defile of the Jiradi pass, then raced for the Suez Canal while Egyptian columns disintegrated in the desert. Jordan, drawn in by the pact and by misleading Egyptian reports of victory, shelled Israeli positions and lost the West Bank within two days; the fight for Ammunition Hill on the northern edge of Jerusalem, a trench system taken at close quarters, became the war's most retold Israeli battle and preceded the capture of the Old City. On the last two days Israeli troops climbed the Golan escarpment, taking Syrian strongpoints such as Tel Azaziat, and held the plateau when the ceasefire came on 10 June. The war also produced episodes that were buried for decades: the Israeli air and torpedo attack on the American intelligence ship USS Liberty off Sinai on 8 June, which killed 34 US sailors and which Israel called a case of mistaken identity, and the killing of Egyptian prisoners of war at Ras Sedr and elsewhere in Sinai, admitted in later years by an Israeli commander and partly confirmed by a mass grave found in 2000.

The arithmetic of six days was stark. Somewhere between 10,000 and 18,000 Arab soldiers were dead or missing against fewer than a thousand Israelis; Israel held the Sinai, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, roughly tripling the territory under its control. Around 300,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from the West Bank, many of them refugees for the second time since 1948, and about 100,000 Syrians left the Golan. In September Arab leaders met at Khartoum and issued their "three noes" — no peace, no recognition, no negotiation — and in November the UN Security Council passed Resolution 242, with its deliberately ambiguous formula of Israeli withdrawal from occupied territory in exchange for recognition and secure borders. Both documents have shaped every negotiation since.
significance: Six days redrew the political map of the Middle East and created the situation the region still lives in. The occupation that began in June 1967 — of the West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem and the Golan — is the direct origin of the settlement enterprise, of the legal and territorial disputes at the center of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and of the "land for peace" framework that produced the Egyptian-Israeli treaty in 1979 and stalled almost everywhere else. The defeat discredited Nasser's pan-Arabism and the secular nationalist project across the Arab world, opening room for both Palestinian nationalism as an independent force and, over the following decade, for Islamist movements that argued secular nationalism had failed. It bound the United States and Israel into a close strategic partnership, deepened Soviet commitment to Egypt and Syria, and set up the rematch of 1973. For Israelis it produced an intoxicating sense of deliverance and, for many, a lasting messianic reading of the territorial gains; for Palestinians it produced a second mass displacement and the beginning of an occupation now measured in generations.
coverage: Written from standard reference accounts (Britannica, Wikipedia) and the US State Department's Office of the Historian, supplemented by Israeli and Egyptian material on the Ras Sedr killings. The seven events in this dataset are almost all set-piece battles told from the Israeli side, where unit histories and archives are rich; Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian operational records are far less accessible, and civilian experience — the flight from the West Bank and Golan, life in Gaza and Sinai during the fighting — is barely represented here. Two things remain genuinely contested rather than merely thin: whether the Israeli first strike was defensive necessity or a chosen opportunity for expansion, on which serious historians still disagree, and the scale of the killing of Egyptian prisoners, where Israeli military historian Aryeh Yitzhaki's archive-based estimate of about a thousand, Egyptian human rights claims of hundreds more at El Arish, and official Israeli silence cannot be reconciled from the public record.
